final_result.title: Impact of contour on aesthetic judgments and approach-avoidance decisions in architecture

findings.quote: Participants were significantly more likely to judge spaces as beautiful if they were curvilinear than rectilinear (χ2 = 2.15, P < 0.005).
In contrast, contour had no effect on approach-avoidance decisions (χ2 = 0.27, P = 0.21) (Fig. 2).
Pleasantness was once again a significant predictor of beauty judgments (β = 0.30, P < 0.001).
Pleasantness also became a significant predictor of approach-avoidance decisions (β = 0.26, P < 0.001).
Pleasantness ratings accounted for 58% of the observed variance in beauty ratings.
Pleasantness ratings accounted for 59% of the observed variance in approach-avoidance decisions.
Our results demonstrated that participants viewed spaces that they chose to “enter” for longer periods compared with spaces that they opted to “exit,” t(17) = 2.60, P < 0.05 (Fig. 4).
In addition, there was no difference in reaction time between “beautiful” and “not beautiful” judgments, t(17) = 0.84, P = 0.41.
There was no difference in reaction time between approach-avoidance decisions (t(17) = 1.29, P = 0.21).
The contrast of curvilinear-rectilinear spaces revealed significant activation in ACC (curvilinear > rectilinear: Z = 4.54, x = 10, y = 62, z = 6) (Fig. 5).

The contrast of curvilinear-rectilinear contours revealed significant activation in the visual cortex that included left lingual gyrus (Z = 3.85, x = −20, y = −94, z = −8) (Fig. 6).
regions within the right calcarine (Z = 3.71, x = 2, y = −76, z = −4 and Z = 3.62, x = 10, y = −74, z = −2) (Fig. 6).
Finally, we did not find any significant activation in the amygdala in the approach-avoidance run.

mechanisms: Neuroscientific data elucidates underlying mechanisms of architectural features on behavior.
Neural underpinnings of visual perception, spatial navigation, and memory influence responses to architecture.
Habitat theory: aesthetic satisfaction from natural landscapes signals environmental conditions favorable for survival.
Features evolved for natural habitats continue to influence interactions with constructed spaces.
Aesthetic judgments activate a distributed neural network, including reward and affective circuitry.
Curvilinear forms are experienced as softer and more pleasant; angular forms as harder and more serious.
Impact of contour on preference for curvilinear objects is driven by an affective response.
The ACC forms a functional network underlying sensory, reward, and affective processing.
The ACC acts as an intermediary linking aesthetic judgment of beauty for curvilinear spaces to reward and emotion.
Emotional valence modulates the preference for curved objects.
The amygdala is involved in the processing of threat.
limitations: The observed effects might be context-dependent, as built environments and landscapes may not be comparable in promoting biological survival.
Manipulating contour in landscapes might impact approach decisions and neural correlates differently than in built environments.
Further experimentation is needed to definitively determine the degree of overlap between neural bases of beauty judgments and approach-avoidance decisions.
No available dataset of architectural stimuli existed that provided 100 rectilinear and 100 curvilinear images, balanced for ceiling height and openness, necessitating custom stimulus creation.

final_result.title: The impact of room shape on affective states, heartrate, and creative output

findings.quote: Participants reported significantly higher scores on positive affect for the curved-room condition (M = 30.60, SD = 6.72) compared to the rectangular-room condition (M = 23.94, SD = 8.69, t(34) = 4.87, p < 0.001), with a large effect size (Cohen's d = 0.82).

participants had significantly higher negative affect scores for the rectangular-room condition (M = 12.62, SD = 3.80) compared to the curved-room condition (M = 11.51, SD = 1.99, t(34) = 2.09, p = .04), with a small effect size (Cohen's d = 0.35).

Participants had a significantly lower heart rate for the curved-room condition (M = 76.67, SD = 8.76) compared to the rectangular-room condition (M = 83.58, SD = 6.68, t(33) = 4.18, p < 0.001), with a medium effect size (Cohen's d = 0.71).

Participants had a significantly higher SemDis scores for the curved-room condition (M = 4.37, SD = 1.68) compared to the rectangular-room condition (M = 3.63, SD = 1.55), t(34) = 2.06, p < 0.047), with a small effect size (Cohen's d = 0.35).

mechanisms: Curved architectural spaces are associated with feelings of safety, pleasantness, and reduced threat, leading to higher positive emotional responses.
Angular geometry and rectangular interior spaces can elicit a more threatening response.
Humans have an inherent inclination to approach environments that evoke positive emotions and avoid those perceived as unfriendly or threatening.
Curvature preference may stem from its ubiquity in natural settings.
Lower resting heart rate is associated with subjective feelings of relaxation and comfort, as well as positive affect.
Neurophysiological positive emotional response to curved room conditions (fMRI and EEG findings from prior research).
Various room features (window views of nature, complexity, natural materials, warmer colours) can enhance creative thinking.
Associative theory of creativity: creative thinking involves linking remote concepts in semantic memory.
limitations: GAUT and semantic distance may not be the most sensitive measures of creativity; other instruments are available.
Study focused only on rectangular versus curved geometry; future studies should explore various room shapes and curved walls.
Potential moderating impact of other factors, such as participant personality, requires further research.

mechanisms: Blue-light-induced reduction in NREM EEG power density in the SWA range could be through its possible alerting effects.
Alerting properties of light during wakefulness rely crucially upon factors such as prior wakefulness, environmental light history and endogenous circadian phase.
Sleep is regulated by the interaction of a homeostatic and a circadian component.
Acute light-induction of sleep in mice seems to be modulated by the melanopsin-based photoreception, reflecting a strong photic input to sleep.

Neuronal networks underlying responses to light involve intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells that project onto the suprachiasmatic nuclei (SCN), subparaventricular zone and the ventrolateral pre-optic area (VLPO).
The VLPO innervates the major nuclei of the ascending monoaminergic and histaminergic pathways implicated in wakefulness.

Galanin- and gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA)-releasing neurons within the VLPO have been characterized as sleep-active neurons that may promote sleep actively by inhibiting the ascending arousal systems.
Blue-enriched light may elicit a stronger wake-promoting signal onto the SCN and VLPO, by shifting the balance of the inhibitory interaction towards sleep promotion and arousal inhibition.

Homeostatic increase in the SWA range is most predominant in the frontal cortex, indicating a higher vulnerability of this brain area to increased sleep pressure or neuronal tiredness due to use-dependent factors, such as synaptic overload.
Blue-enriched light may counteract the increased susceptibility of the frontal cortex to higher sleep pressure.
Light-induced reduction in accumulated sleep pressure, as indexed by less frontal NREM SWA.
Melanopsin (and also rods and cones) photo-pigment system achieve a stable state of photo-equilibrium through a reduction in the 'bleaching effect' of previous light exposure.
limitations: Absence of a control night (no light pulses) makes the extent to which light affects sleep structure and sleep EEG power density unclear.
Individual prior light history was not controlled, so its effects cannot be ruled out.
The study tested only acute effects of light on sleep, not allowing for assessment of long-term effects of chronic light exposure.
Generalizing results to real-life conditions should be done with caution due to stringent control for 'photic memory'.
